templates.name: Modifier placement: past participial opener (incl. Compared with that of)
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb
Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner its/their vs contractions
Subject-verb agreement, relative pronoun or possessive inside subject
Subject-verb agreement, quantifier or compound subject
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive (purpose or after “the first”)

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (By + -ing), passage-final blank; the physicist is the right subject
items.passage: In 1947, a team of physicists at England’s University of Bristol, including Brazilian physicist César Lattes, was searching for a short-lived particle that theorists had predicted but no experiment had yet detected. By exposing special photographic plates to cosmic rays high on Bolivia’s Mount Chacaltaya, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: clear evidence of the particle, which is now known as the pion, was collected by Lattes.
Lattes’s plates provided clear evidence of the particle, which is now known as the pion.
Lattes collected clear evidence of the particle, which is now known as the pion.
it was Lattes who collected clear evidence of the particle, which is now known as the pion.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “By exposing special photographic plates to cosmic rays high on Bolivia’s Mount Chacaltaya,” describes someone who exposed the plates: the physicist. Choice C places “Lattes” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that Lattes is the one who exposed the plates and collected the evidence.

A.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
A.why_wrong: “Clear evidence” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the evidence exposed the photographic plates to cosmic rays.

B.why_wrong: The subject is “Lattes’s plates,” not Lattes, so the sentence illogically says that the plates exposed themselves to cosmic rays and then provided the evidence.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the opening phrase has nothing it can logically describe; the person who exposed the plates appears only later, inside the clause.

items.notes: Subject: César Lattes and the 1947 pion plates from Mount Chacaltaya (science, physics). Real physicist; facts kept general (Bristol team, plates exposed on Chacaltaya, evidence of the pion). Band 6 as 188f7e3c (passage-final blank after a By + gerund opener) with the E and P recipes of dfbf5d33 (3.15); recipes V, P, E. The P foil names the plates, the thing exposed, so it cannot be read as the agent. Key is the shortest option, not the longest.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: Plan band 6. Plain agent key (Lattes) after a By + gerund opener with V, P and E foils, as 188f7e3c and dfbf5d33; not the property-key setting of band 7. Checked against CoE w2b6_19 (Chacaltaya observatory row) and FSS w4b4_01 (cosmic-ray muons at Giza): different subjects.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Carved from ... and paid for ...), passage-final blank; the sculpture is the right subject
items.passage: Egyptian sculptor Mahmoud Mokhtar studied sculpture in Paris before returning to Cairo, where in 1928 he unveiled the monumental work that established him as a national figure. Carved from pink granite quarried near Aswan and financed partly through contributions from the public, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the sculpture Egypt’s Awakening depicts a peasant woman lifting her veil beside a sphinx rising to its feet.
Mokhtar depicted a peasant woman lifting her veil beside a sphinx rising to its feet in his sculpture Egypt’s Awakening.
a peasant woman is depicted in Egypt’s Awakening lifting her veil beside a sphinx rising to its feet.
there is a peasant woman in Egypt’s Awakening who lifts her veil beside a sphinx rising to its feet.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Carved from pink granite quarried near Aswan and financed partly through contributions from the public,” describes the work itself. Choice A places “the sculpture Egypt’s Awakening” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the sculpture is what was carved from granite and financed by the public.

B.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the sculptor
B.why_wrong: “Mokhtar” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the sculptor himself was carved from pink granite and financed by the public.

C.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V): the figure shown
C.why_wrong: “A peasant woman” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the woman depicted, rather than the sculpture, was financed partly through contributions from the public.

D.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, so the phrase has no noun it can logically describe; the sculpture appears only inside a later phrase.

items.notes: Subject: Mahmoud Mokhtar’s granite monument Egypt’s Awakening (Nahdet Masr), unveiled in Cairo in 1928 (arts, sculpture). Real artist and work; facts kept general (training in Paris, pink Aswan granite, public subscription, peasant woman lifting her veil beside a sphinx rising to its feet). Band 6 as b369d54c and f0864217: a thing (the work) is the right subject after a participial opener; the second participle (“financed partly through contributions from the public”) rules out the figure in C. Key is not the longest option. Recipes W, V, E.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: Plan band 6. Thing key (the sculpture) after a two-part participial opener, as b369d54c and f0864217; the second participle (financed by the public) is what rules out the depicted woman in C.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a long subject holding its own relative clauses (that ... implemented, which included ...)
items.passage: In late 1910, an epidemic of pneumonic plague began spreading along the railways of northeastern China. The measures that Malayan-born physician Wu Lien-teh implemented, which included strict quarantines, restrictions on rail travel, and masks made of cotton and gauze, ______ bring the outbreak under control by the spring of 1911.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is “The measures,” and everything up to the blank describes those measures, including two relative clauses (“that ... implemented” and “which included ...”). The sentence still needs a main verb for “The measures.” Choice D supplies the finite past tense verb “helped,” so the sentence says what the measures did.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: to + base
A.why_wrong: The infinitive “to help” cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence, so the sentence would be a fragment with no main verb for “The measures.”

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: -ing
B.why_wrong: The participle “helping” cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence, so the sentence would be a fragment with no main verb for “The measures.”

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: having + past participle
C.why_wrong: The phrase “having helped” is nonfinite and cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence would have no main verb for “The measures.”

items.notes: Subject: Wu Lien-teh and the 1910 to 1911 Manchurian pneumonic plague (science, medicine and history). Real physician; facts kept general (quarantines, rail restrictions, cotton-and-gauze masks, outbreak controlled by spring 1911). Band 6 as a75d5984 (3.13): canonical option set {finite, to + base, -ing, having + participle}; the subject is held open for 26 words by a restrictive and a nonrestrictive relative clause whose own finite verbs (implemented, included) can make a reader feel the clause already has its verb. No dash list, so the model’s skeleton is not copied.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official item (band7 appendix), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 as a75d5984, with the head 26 words before the blank behind two relative clauses that have their own finite verbs.

items.subtype: Possessive determiner 20 words before its plural antecedent (Yet with ______ ..., the films ...), singular nouns between and a singular film title before the verb
items.passage: Filipino director Lino Brocka made more than sixty films, many of them low-budget projects for commercial studios. Yet with ______ unsparing portraits of life in Manila’s poorest neighborhoods, such as the crowded district of Tondo, the films he made on his own terms, among them Insiang (1976), earned him international acclaim.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank comes before the noun it refers to: the phrase “with ______ unsparing portraits of life in Manila’s poorest neighborhoods, such as the crowded district of Tondo” describes the subject of the sentence, “the films he made on his own terms.” Because “films” is plural, the plural possessive determiner “their” is needed. The singular nouns in between (“life,” “the crowded district,” “Tondo”) and the single title “Insiang,” an example set off by commas, cannot own the portraits.

A.recipe: wrong-number determiner matching the nearest singular noun
A.why_wrong: The singular “its” does not agree with the plural noun “films,” the subject the phrase describes; it may seem to fit a nearby singular noun such as “Tondo” or the single film “Insiang,” but neither owns the portraits.

C.why_wrong: “It’s” is the contraction of “it is” or “it has,” not a possessive, and it is also singular.

D.why_wrong: “They’re” is the contraction of “they are,” not a possessive determiner, so it cannot show that the portraits belong to the films.

items.notes: Subject: Lino Brocka’s films, Insiang (1976) (arts, film). Real director; facts kept general (more than sixty films, many low-budget commercial projects, slum portraits, Tondo as the setting of Insiang per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insiang, Insiang). Band 7 on 0bcb4417’s frame (determiner before a plural antecedent): reviewer moved “the films” 16 words past the blank with the singular nouns life, Manila, district and Tondo between, and Insiang between head and verb. Only “their” is grammatical: no singular noun can own the portraits.
band7_moves: determiner before its antecedent (band-7 file, section 3 move 8, as 0bcb4417): “With ______ ... portraits” resolves to “the films” 11 words later
singular attractors in the window: “life,” “Manila’s,” and the single title “Insiang (1976)” set off by commas right before the verb, so “its” reads well until the head noun is found
the previous sentence counts films but uses no plural pronoun, so nothing outside the sentence settles the number
options the 2 x 2 grid (its, their, it’s, they’re) as in both band-7 models

fixes: moved the antecedent 16 words past the blank (added “such as the crowded district of Tondo,” “Yet” for “however,” “international acclaim” for the longer close) so the item reaches the 0bcb4417 setting; Tondo checked against en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insiang (set and shot there); explanation and A rationale updated
review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: As 0bcb4417 after the fix: the determiner sits 16 words before its plural antecedent (the films), past the singular nouns life, Manila, district and Tondo, with the singular title Insiang between head and verb; 2 x 2 grid. As drafted the antecedent was 12 words away with no singular noun near it, which read band 6.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular possessor before a plural head (The novel’s secondary characters), singular nouns in the intervener
items.passage: Toji (Land), South Korean novelist Park Kyong-ni’s sprawling five-part saga, follows the Choi family, wealthy landowners in a southern village, from 1897 to 1945. The novel’s secondary characters, such as a household servant or a peddler traveling from one rural market to another, ______ the story of a single family into a panoramic portrait of a changing society.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is “The novel’s secondary characters.” Its head noun is the plural “characters”; “The novel’s” is a singular possessor, and “a household servant,” “a peddler,” and “one rural market” sit inside the interrupting phrase. The plural verb “turn” agrees with “characters.”

A.why_wrong: The singular verb “turns” agrees with the possessor “novel’s” or with “a peddler,” not with the plural head noun “characters.”

B.why_wrong: The singular verb “is turning” does not agree with the plural subject “characters.”

D.why_wrong: The singular verb “has turned” does not agree with the plural subject “characters.”

items.notes: Subject: Park Kyong-ni’s saga novel Toji (Land), 1897 to 1945 (literature). Real novel; facts kept general (five-part saga, the landowning Choi family of a southern village, the years covered). Band 6: singular possessor before a plural head, as f10b7ce4, but with a plain intervener (no inverted frame and no intervener verb of the other number), and 17 words from the head to the blank with four singular nouns between. Key plural; three singular foils in three tenses.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: Plan band 6. Singular possessor before a plural head with four singular nouns in the intervener, the f10b7ce4 setting, but no intervener verb of the other number, so a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: absolute phrase after a complete clause (its tiny fronds, each ..., ______), finite foils make comma splices
items.passage: Wolffia globosa, a rootless aquatic plant that floats on still water, is among the smallest flowering plants on Earth. In Thailand and Laos, it has traditionally been harvested from ponds and incorporated into omelets and curries, its tiny fronds, each roughly the size of a pinhead, ______ substantial amounts of protein, dietary fiber, and essential minerals.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The words before “its tiny fronds” already form a complete sentence, so the phrase that follows must be a supplement, not a second independent clause. The nonfinite participle “supplying” forms that supplement: an absolute phrase built on “its tiny fronds,” describing what the plant offers as food.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed: comma splice (present perfect)
A.why_wrong: The finite verb “have supplied” turns “its tiny fronds ... have supplied substantial amounts” into a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed: comma splice (present progressive)
B.why_wrong: The finite verb “are supplying” makes the phrase a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed: comma splice (simple present)
C.why_wrong: The finite verb “supply” makes “its tiny fronds ... supply substantial amounts” a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: Wolffia globosa eaten in Thailand and Laos (science, botany and food). No named people. Facts kept general (rootless, among the smallest flowering plants, harvested from ponds and used in omelets and curries, a source of protein, fiber and minerals). Band 7 on the absolute-phrase setting of 81f09e07 and c88ba1b7, not the trailing -ing result phrase of a30567fd. Reviewer: the drafted foils (had supplied, were supplying, supplied) were all past tense beside the passage’s present perfect, so each also failed on tense; now present perfect, present progressive and simple present, so only the comma splice rules them out.
band7_moves: absolute phrase after a complete clause (band-7 file, section 3 move 3, as 81f09e07): the possessive noun phrase “its tiny fronds” before the blank lets every finite option form a full clause, so the error is a comma splice, not a missing subject
an appositive interrupter (“each roughly the size of a pinhead”) between the absolute phrase’s noun and the blank hides that a clause has already ended
the finite foils are past perfect, past progressive and simple past, as in 81f09e07; the -ed foil cannot read as a reduced relative (“fronds ... supplied substantial amounts” has no passive sense)

fixes: replaced past-tense foils (had supplied, were supplying, supplied) with present-family ones (have supplied, are supplying, supply) so tense no longer gives the key away; rationales updated
review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: As 81f09e07 and c88ba1b7: complete clause, comma, possessive noun, an appositive (each roughly the size of a pinhead), blank. After the fix every finite foil is present-family, matching the present perfect clause, so each fails only as a comma splice, not also on tense.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: quantifier head (each of the 27 observation stations, which were distributed ...), plural relative-clause verb before the blank
items.passage: Adopted in China in 1281, the Shoushi calendar fixed the year at 365.2425 days, the value the Gregorian calendar would use three centuries later. To gather the necessary observations, astronomer Guo Shoujing organized a survey in which each of the 27 observation stations, which were distributed from the South China Sea to Siberia, ______ responsible for measuring noon shadows and the altitude of the pole star above the horizon.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the clause with the blank is “each of the 27 observation stations.” Its head is “each,” which is singular: the sentence describes what every single station had to do. The plural noun “stations” and the plural verb “were distributed” belong to the phrase and the relative clause that come between, so the singular verb “was” is needed.

B.recipe: wrong number (plural), past: agrees with the intervener
B.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” agrees with “stations” and echoes “were distributed,” but the head of the subject is the singular “each.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” does not agree with the singular subject “each.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “each.”

items.notes: Subject: Guo Shoujing’s survey for the Shoushi calendar (history of science, astronomy). Real astronomer and calendar; facts kept general (adopted 1281, 365.2425-day year, 27 stations from the South China Sea to Siberia measuring noon shadows and the pole star’s altitude). Band 7: quantifier head plus plural intervener verb, as 0fe5ce68 and 5fd86f4b, but with “each of” rather than their “each one of,” a past-tense be-family set, and no contrast tag (c7cb5186’s compound frame not reused).
band7_moves: quantifier head with a plural relative clause in the intervener (band-7 file, section 3 move 4, as 0fe5ce68): “each of the 27 observation stations, which were distributed ...” puts a plural verb that agrees with the attractor right before the blank, so the wrong number sounds right twice
15 run words after the blank (“responsible for measuring ... above the horizon”), so the clause stays open well past the verb
the clause is buried inside a “survey in which” relative clause after a singular main clause, so the subject is not the first noun of the sentence
options the be-family in past, present and present perfect, wrong number only in the foils

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: As 0fe5ce68: quantifier head each of + plural noun, a relative clause whose own verb (were) is foil B, 14 run words after the blank; every foil agrees with the attractor.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical verb: singular head (The palette) behind an of-phrase and a participial phrase full of plurals
items.passage: Venezuelan painter Armando Reverón did most of his work in Macuto, a coastal village where he constructed a home and studio from stone, wood, and palm leaves. The palette of his landscapes from the 1920s, dominated by luminous whites and pale yellows, ______ the overwhelming brilliance of tropical sunlight.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is “The palette,” which is singular; “of his landscapes from the 1920s” and “dominated by luminous whites and pale yellows” describe it. The singular verb “captures” agrees with “palette.”

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “capture” agrees with “landscapes” or “yellows,” not with the singular subject “palette.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are capturing” does not agree with the singular subject “palette.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have captured” does not agree with the singular subject “palette.”

items.notes: Subject: Armando Reverón’s pale coastal landscapes, Macuto (arts, painting). Real painter; facts kept general (worked mostly in Macuto, a self-built home of stone, wood and palm leaves, 1920s landscapes dominated by whites). Medium as 2.7 and 2.20: singular head with a plural of-phrase and a participial phrase holding two more plurals.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: singular possessor + plural noun (the composer’s pieces), partial 2 x 2 grid
items.passage: Paraguayan guitarist Agustín Barrios Mangoré, who began recording around 1910, was among the first classical guitarists whose performances were preserved on disc. Because he published relatively little of his music, many of the ______ survived only in handwritten copies or on recordings until decades after his death in 1944.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pieces belong to one composer, Barrios Mangoré, so the singular possessive “composer’s” is needed. “Many of the ... survived” calls for more than one piece, and nothing belongs to the pieces, so the plain plural “pieces” is correct.

A.why_wrong: “Composers” is a plain plural, not a possessive, so it does not show that the pieces belong to Barrios Mangoré.

B.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
B.why_wrong: “Composer’s” is right, but “piece’s” is a singular possessive; the pieces do not own anything, so a plain plural is needed.

D.recipe: wrong possessor number and needless apostrophe
D.why_wrong: “Composers’” is a plural possessive, but the pieces belong to one composer, and “pieces’” wrongly makes the pieces possessive.

items.notes: Subject: Agustín Barrios Mangoré’s guitar music (arts, music). Real guitarist; facts kept general (recorded from around 1910, among the first classical guitarists on disc, little published, died 1944). Medium as 2.24: a single named person sets the possessor’s number; partial grid with one missing apostrophe, one needless apostrophe and one wrong possessor number.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Tense: simple past for a completed span ending in a dated past event (for about five decades, until ... in 1944)
items.passage: Telefon Hírmondó, founded in Budapest in 1893, was a newspaper that subscribers listened to rather than read: announcers with loud voices read the news over telephone lines on a fixed daily schedule. The service ______ news, stock prices, and concerts to its subscribers for about five decades, until it shut down in 1944.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The service was “founded in Budapest in 1893” and ran “until it shut down in 1944,” so the span of about five decades lies wholly in the past. The simple past “delivered” matches that completed span and the past tense of the first sentence.

B.why_wrong: The future “will deliver” describes a later time, but the service ended in 1944.

C.recipe: present simple where the past is needed
C.why_wrong: The present “delivers” describes something still happening, but the service shut down in 1944.

D.recipe: present perfect progressive where the past is needed
D.why_wrong: “Has been delivering” describes an activity continuing up to now, but the service stopped in 1944.

items.notes: Subject: Telefon Hírmondó, the Budapest telephone newspaper, 1893 to 1944 (history, technology). Reviewer replacement: the drafted Kadambini Ganguly item repeated live form_structure_and_sense.R2_to_inf.easy.w2b1_22 (Anandibai Joshi, studies completed 1886, early Indian woman in Western medicine). Facts from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telefon_Hírmondó (founded 1893, loud-voiced announcers, daily programme listings, stock quotations, concerts, terminated 1944). Medium: the cue is a span closed by a date in the same sentence; the present perfect progressive foil fails only because the span has ended.

fixes: replaced the subject: Kadambini Ganguly cloned live w2b1_22 (Anandibai Joshi, 1886); new passage on Telefon Hírmondó (1893 to 1944), same template, key A; re-solved blind: A
review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family: singular head + appositive with plural nouns and a plural relative-clause verb
items.passage: The spotted handfish, one of several bottom-dwelling fishes that move across the seafloor on fins resembling human hands, ______ found exclusively in the estuary of Tasmania’s Derwent River and a few neighboring bays, where its numbers have declined sharply since the 1980s.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is “The spotted handfish,” a single kind of fish; the phrase between the first two commas describes it. The singular verb “is” agrees with “handfish,” and the present tense suits a current fact about where it lives.

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” agrees with “fishes” or “fins” inside the interrupting phrase, not with the singular subject “handfish.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “handfish.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” does not agree with the singular subject “handfish.”

items.notes: Subject: spotted handfish of the Derwent estuary, Tasmania (science, zoology). No named people. Medium as 2.21: singular head + appositive full of plurals; the appositive’s own relative verb (“that move”) is plural. Facts kept general (Derwent estuary and nearby bays, decline since the 1980s).

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener (One of the first scientists to ...), mid-sentence blank; the scientist is the right subject
items.passage: One of the first scientists to study the fossil plants of the Indian subcontinent systematically, ______ in Lucknow in 1946. The institute, which now bears his name, remains a leading center for research on prehistoric plant life.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the Institute of Palaeobotany was founded by Birbal Sahni
Birbal Sahni founded the Institute of Palaeobotany
it was Birbal Sahni who founded the Institute of Palaeobotany
Birbal Sahni’s Institute of Palaeobotany was founded
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “One of the first scientists to study the fossil plants of the Indian subcontinent systematically,” describes a person. Choice B places “Birbal Sahni” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that Sahni is the scientist being described.

A.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
A.why_wrong: “The Institute of Palaeobotany” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the institute was one of the first scientists to study fossil plants.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase describing a scientist has no noun it can logically describe.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “Birbal Sahni’s Institute of Palaeobotany,” not Sahni, so the sentence illogically says that the institute was one of the first scientists.

items.notes: Subject: Birbal Sahni and the Institute of Palaeobotany, Lucknow, 1946 (science, paleobotany). Real scientist; facts kept general (early systematic study of the subcontinent’s fossil plants, institute founded 1946, now named for him). Medium as 2.10 (appositive opener, mid-sentence blank, person as subject), with a different opener (“One of the first scientists to”) so the model’s “A pioneer in” frame is not copied. Recipes V, E, P. Key is the shortest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a general process (When someone eats ..., ... taste sweet)
items.passage: The miracle berry, the small red fruit of a shrub native to West Africa, contains a protein called miraculin. When someone eats the berry, miraculin ______ to the taste receptors that detect sweetness, so for some time afterward, acidic foods such as lemons taste surprisingly sweet.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text describes something that happens in general whenever the berry is eaten: “When someone eats the berry” and “acidic foods ... taste surprisingly sweet” are both in the simple present. The simple present “binds” matches.

A.recipe: simple past where present is needed
A.why_wrong: The past tense “bound” describes one past event, but the text describes what generally happens whenever someone eats the berry.

B.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
B.why_wrong: The past perfect “had bound” places the action before another past event, but the text describes a general process in the present.

D.why_wrong: The past progressive “was binding” describes an action in progress at a past moment, not a general process in the present.

items.notes: Subject: miracle berry (Synsepalum dulcificum) and miraculin (science, food chemistry). No named people. Easy as 1.37: general present process, present-tense cues in the same sentence.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a recurring custom (During each festival, ... dance)
items.passage: Gèlèdé, a masquerade performed by Yoruba communities in Benin and Nigeria, celebrates the power of women, especially mothers and female elders. During each festival, male performers ______ carved and brightly painted wooden headdresses and dance in the marketplace to the rhythms of drums.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text describes something that happens at every festival: “During each festival” is a repeated, present-day custom, and the parallel verb “dance” is in the simple present. The simple present “wear” matches.

B.recipe: simple past where present is needed
B.why_wrong: The past tense “wore” does not match the present-tense custom described by “celebrates” and the parallel verb “dance.”

C.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
C.why_wrong: The past perfect “had worn” places the action before a past event, but the text describes a recurring present custom.

D.why_wrong: The past progressive “were wearing” describes a single past moment, not a custom repeated at each festival.
